passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A mitten and a careful look
passages.text: Nia reached into her coat pocket and found only one mitten. She looked under the bench. A red leaf lay there, curled like a tiny hand. Nia nearly cried. Grandpa asked, "Where did you take your coat off?" Nia remembered the warm bus. Then she remembered carrying her coat over her arm. She checked the other pocket. There was the mitten, tucked beside her snack. "I looked everywhere except the other pocket!" she said. Grandpa smiled. Nia put on both mittens and left the leaf where it was.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
A Lost-and-Found Tray
Our classroom has a shallow tray beside the door. Small lost things go in the tray. Large things, such as coats, hang on hooks above it. If you find an object, tell an adult before moving it. If you have lost something, describe it before taking it. A blue pencil may belong to more than one child. A name on an object can help its owner find it. On Friday, the teacher holds up the remaining objects so everyone can look.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The little bridge
passages.text: Ravi and Mei built a bridge across a pretend river made from a blue scarf. They rested a strip of card on two blocks. When Ravi rolled a toy truck onto it, the card sagged into the river. Mei slid another block under the middle. "Now the truck has somewhere firm to stand," she said. Ravi tried again. This time the truck crossed. They made a sign that said BRIDGE OPEN. Then Mei asked whether two trucks could cross together. Ravi reached for another truck instead of pretending he already knew.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Testing a Paper Bridge
Lay a strip of paper across two equal stacks of books. Keep the stacks close enough that both ends of the paper rest on them. Place one small block in the middle. Watch what happens. Take the block away before changing the bridge. Fold a second strip like a fan and put it across the same gap. Try the same block again. Using the same gap and block makes the two trials easier to compare. Record what you see, even if your prediction was different.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Room for a song
passages.text: Every child in the little singing group chose one sound for their song. Dax chose a booming drum sound. Elle chose a bright clap. Mina chose a tiny hum, softer than a buzzing bee. The group began together. Nobody could hear Mina. "Sing louder!" Dax said. Mina tried, but her hum disappeared again. Elle held up a hand. "What if we become quieter?" she asked. On the next try, Dax tapped his knees and Elle brushed her palms. Mina’s hum floated between their sounds. They kept that part in the song.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
A Rehearsal Card
Before our group sings, we stand where we can see the leader. When the leader raises a hand, we get ready. When the hand moves down, we begin. We stop when the leader closes a fist. These signals let everyone start and stop together. During practice, one person may listen while the others sing. The listener tells which sounds were clear. Then the group can change its volume, which means how loud or soft the sounds are.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A seed label mix-up
passages.text: Tomas planted two pots, one with bean seeds and one with pea seeds. He meant to write labels after lunch. When he returned, both pots looked exactly alike: dark soil in brown cups. "This one is beans," he guessed, pointing left. His sister asked how he knew. Tomas stared at the cups, then shook his head. "I don’t know yet." They placed a card between the pots: WAIT AND WATCH. Tomas made labels before planting his next two cups. He wanted a record he could trust, not a very confident guess.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Label Before You Plant
For this classroom activity, put a blank label beside each empty pot. Write the seed’s name on the label while the seed packet is still beside you. Attach the label to the pot. Add soil and plant that kind of seed, following the packet’s directions with an adult. Put the packet away only after checking the label. The label records what you planted. A date on the label can also show when you planted it. Keep the writing readable when you water.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The shelter of the shed
passages.text: Rain tapped the roof of the play shed. Luis stood outside because every dry seat seemed full. Ada noticed his wet sleeves. She moved the basket of wooden blocks from the bench to the shelf. "There’s room here," she called. Luis sat beside her. He did not say much, but he took a small cloth from his pocket and wiped the puddle he had brought in. When another child appeared at the doorway, Luis slid closer to Ada. This time he was the one who called, "There’s room here."

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Keeping the Play Shed Ready
The shed has a bench for sitting, a shelf for baskets, and a clear doorway for walking in and out. Put blocks back into their basket after play. Keep the basket on the shelf so the bench stays open. If rainwater makes a puddle on the floor, tell an adult. The adult can help dry it. Leave the doorway clear, even when you are waiting for a turn. These routines make room for people and help everyone use the space.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A gift with a purpose
passages.text: Owen made a beautiful bookmark for his aunt. He covered it with thick buttons, soft feathers, and a shiny shell. When Aunt Jo tried to close her book, the pages would not lie flat. Owen’s smile vanished. "It’s lovely to look at," she said, "but a bookmark has a job." Together they moved the decorations onto a card for her wall. Owen cut a thin strip of paper and drew a tiny shell on it. That strip slipped between the pages easily. Aunt Jo hung the bright card above her chair and put the new bookmark into her book.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Make a Useful Bookmark
Choose a thin piece of card or firm paper. Cut a strip with an adult’s help if needed. Draw a small design on it. Keep the surface flat: thick objects can stop a book from closing neatly. passages.text: Jo pulled the garden cart toward the shed. A puddle spread across the short path, but Jo kept going. One wheel sank into mud. The tray of seedlings tilted. passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The puppet’s missing voice
passages.text: Behind a curtain in the classroom, Bea held up her sock puppet. Her partner, Kian, waited with a cardboard crown. The audience settled on the rug. Bea opened the puppet’s mouth, but no words came out of her own mouth. Kian quietly made his puppet bow. "Our visitor is thinking," he announced. Bea took a breath. She whispered the first line, then spoke the second more clearly. By the end, both puppets were arguing cheerfully about who should wear the crown. After the curtain closed, Bea thanked Kian for giving her a moment.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A ramp for the marble
passages.text: Lena set a marble at the top of her cardboard ramp. It rolled down quickly, bounced off the table, and disappeared beneath a cupboard. Her friend Max fetched it with a long ruler while their teacher watched. Lena tried to hold her hands at the bottom of the ramp, but she wanted a design that could catch the marble by itself. Max folded the end of an empty tray upward. They placed the tray below the ramp. On the next try, the marble rolled into the tray and stopped against the folded edge. Lena drew the change in her plan.

Page 1: Materials

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The lunch cloth rescue
passages.text: At the picnic table, Poppy reached for a plum and knocked over her water cup. Water crept toward Arun’s drawing. Poppy froze with the plum in her hand. Arun lifted his paper onto the bench. "The picture is safe," he said. "Can you get the cloth?" Poppy hurried to the basket and returned with it. They wiped the table together. Poppy expected Arun to be cross, but he asked her to hold the corner of the drawing while it dried in the breeze. She stayed beside him until they could roll it up safely.

Page 3: Packing Away

passages.text: The children were leaving the garden when Nora noticed that Ben was not with them. She looked along the fence, but tall sunflowers hid the far bench and the small gate beside it. Then she heard a faint ting. Ben had been testing the little bell beside the gate. Nora followed the sound and found him kneeling beside the post, tying the loose string back on. "I wanted the next visitor to reach it," he explained. Nora waited while he finished. Together they gave the bell one gentle ring, checked that their teacher could see them, and joined the group.

passages.text: My name is Ivo, and I was carrying the celebration cake. Warm lemon sweetness drifted up from the plate. I wanted everyone to notice how carefully I walked. passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A kite speaking in the wind
passages.text: The kite woke in a rustle of paper. "At last!" it cried as Lila unrolled its tail. I watched from the grassy bank while my little brother held the string. "Who are you?" he whispered to the kite. "A red streak looking for the sky," it replied. Soon it was tugging above us, its tail snapping like a small flag. My brother laughed each time it dipped. I knew the kite’s voice was really Lila’s, but I did not spoil the game. Some afternoons are big enough for a little pretending.

Written information: A kite’s line is the cord a person holds. The tail is a strip or group of strips attached below the kite. A gust is a brief, stronger push of wind. In our activity, an adult chooses an open flying place away from roads, overhead wires, and storms.

passages.text: I thought the music upstairs came from a radio. The same thin tune drifted down every afternoon, then broke off in the same place. passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The rabbit badge
passages.text:
Asha’s paper rabbit badge tore just before the class costume walk. One ear hung by a narrow scrap. She hid the badge in her hand. Mateo offered to throw it away and make another, but there was only a little time. Asha looked at the tear, then at a roll of paper tape. She joined the ear on the back and drew a small hat across the front. "Now my rabbit has a hat," she said. She wore the repaired badge at the front of the line.
Illustration panel, fully described: The badge shows a white rabbit with one ear inside a red pointed hat. A dotted line on a separate back-view panel shows the tape across the tear.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Repair Before Replacing
Try a simple paper repair when the damage is small and an adult says it is suitable. Repairing can save the time of making the whole object again. It can also keep parts of a design you already like. Some damage cannot be fixed well; then making a new object may be sensible.
Illustration panel, fully described: Left, a paper star has a short tear near one point. Right, the same star has a small strip of tape on the back across that tear.
Caption: A small patch joins the two sides.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A robot with a rest sign
passages.text:
Em and Tori took turns being a robot inside a painted box. Other children kept asking it to sing, count, and bow. Inside the box, Em became hot and tired, but the requests did not stop. Tori lifted the side flap and whispered, "You can come out." Then she made a sign for the front. Em stepped out for a drink while Tori pointed to the sign. When they returned, the children asked whether the robot was ready before giving it a job.
Illustration panel, fully described: A cardboard robot has a sliding sign with two windows: READY and RESTING. A blue tab currently covers READY, leaving RESTING visible.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Use a Clear Status Sign
Our pretend station should show whether it is ready or resting. A clear sign helps visitors know when to ask for a turn. It also lets the person inside take a break without repeating the same explanation. The sign needs to change when the situation changes; otherwise it can give visitors the wrong message.
Illustration panel, fully described: Two copies of a sign are shown. One reveals READY; the other reveals RESTING. Arrows connect a hand moving a tab with each visible word.
Caption: Move the tab when the station changes.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The cupcake map
passages.text:
Sami carried a box of cupcakes to the club picnic. Three paths led away from the gate, and each ended near a tree. He could not remember which tree sheltered his group. A volunteer handed him a small map. Sami turned it until the gate on the paper matched the gate behind him. Then he followed the dotted route. His friends cheered when he arrived with the box level and every cake still in place. "The map did the remembering for me," he said.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information

Label a Simple Map
A map for visitors should label important destinations. Labels help a reader tell similar-looking places apart. Show the starting point as well, so readers can connect the paper with where they stand. A route line can show one suggested way to travel. A label alone names a place; it does not tell every turn.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A raincoat for the scarecrow
passages.text:
The class’s miniature scarecrow wore a paper hat that drooped after a splash from the watering can. Nora wanted to make another paper hat, but Eli suggested a cover made from a scrap of waterproof packaging. They tested a small scrap above an empty tray before using it. Water rolled off its sloping sides into the tray. Nora folded the scrap into a little roof and held it over the scarecrow during the next careful watering. The paper hat stayed dry this time.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information

Cover the Paper Model

passages.text:
Each morning, the model-building group spent time searching for its little tools. The ruler hid under scraps, and the brush rolled behind a box. Hana sewed a cloth organizer with help from her uncle. She drew an outline of each tool beside its pocket. On Monday, the brush pocket was empty. Instead of starting a new search everywhere, the children checked the painting table and found the brush in a cup. By cleanup, every outline had a matching tool.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information

Give Each Tool a Place
Keep each classroom tool in a labeled pocket. A fixed place reduces the number of places to search. An outline also helps users notice when a tool is missing. The outline cannot tell where the missing tool went; someone still has to remember or look. Check that each tool fits safely before choosing its pocket.

passages.text:
Story A: The Long Way
Nell reached the tiny stream in the park and saw that the stepping stones were covered with water. She had promised to bring chalk to the drawing group. Rather than try the hidden stones, she followed the marked path to the footbridge. The walk took longer, and her friends had already drawn the first circle when she arrived. Nell handed them the dry chalk. "I brought enough for the next part," she said, and joined them.

passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The Waiting Place
passages.text:
Story B: The Waiting Place
Amir reached a puddle across the school path with a box of paper flags. He could not see how deep the water was. He stood on the dry step and called the teacher. She brought a board approved for the school activity and helped him carry the box along a dry route beside the puddle. Amir’s classmates waited at the door. He gave them the flags and thanked them for leaving room.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Adult read-aloud, not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Keep a Group Together
passages.text:
Information B: Keep a Group Together
Choose a meeting place that everyone can recognize. At a stop, the adult checks that all group members are present before moving on. This check helps prevent someone being left behind. If you cannot see your group, tell a nearby responsible adult rather than wandering to search alone.

passages.text:
Story A: The Checklist
Mia wanted to run the class beanbag game. Before the fair, she listed the bags, the hoops, and a sign. She checked each object as she put it by the door. At the fair, everything was ready except a pencil for keeping scores. Mia borrowed one and added PENCIL to her list. passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Information A: Use a Checklist
A checklist names the things a job needs. Mark each item after checking that it is actually present. This can prevent leaving a needed object behind. Leave room to add an item discovered during the job. A checked box is useful only if someone really checked the object.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The Practice Turn

Story B: The Practice Turn
Leo practised explaining a ring-toss game to his brother. His brother tossed all the rings at once because Leo had not explained turns. Leo changed his speech: one ring, then pass the basket. At the fair, he used the new explanation. A younger player still needed a demonstration, so Leo showed a slow turn before the game continued.

Tell a partner how a game works before a group arrives. Ask the partner to try following your words. A practice turn can reveal a missing step that is hard to notice silently. Change the explanation after watching. Keep a demonstration ready for someone who needs to see the action.

Everyone had put a lunch bag on the bench beside them. When Oona came to the table, every space looked taken. Jules moved his bag under his own feet and asked two friends to do the same. passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Information A: Make Physical Room
Before saying a table is full, check whether bags or unused materials take up seats. Moving those objects to an appropriate storage place can make room for people. Keep walking paths clear when moving them. An invitation works better when there is a usable place to sit.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A Place in the Game
passages.text:
Story B: A Place in the Game
Milo stood beside the board game without touching a piece. There was an empty chair, so Tess asked him to sit. He shook his head. "I don’t know what to do." Tess played one practice turn with him and explained the arrow on the board. On the next turn, Milo moved his own piece. Tess learned that an empty chair was not the only kind of room someone might need.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Adult read-aloud, not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Make the Game Clear
passages.text:
Information B: Make the Game Clear
A new player may need to learn a rule before joining. Offer a practice turn and explain one step at a time. This gives the player a way to try without needing every rule at once. Ask whether the explanation helped instead of assuming a silent player does not want to join.

explanation: The teller’s perspective determines whose thoughts are directly available. passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Messages that arrive differently
passages.text:
Story A: My Note
I wanted Dad to know that our club meeting had moved to the art room. He was on a call, so I wrote ART ROOM, 4 O’CLOCK on a note and put it beside his keys. Later he showed me the note. "Is that today or tomorrow, Sana?" I had forgotten the day. I added TODAY and read the whole message aloud to check it. Dad arrived at the right room that afternoon.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Information A: Leave a Clear Note
A written note can wait for someone who is busy. Include the action, place, and time the reader needs. Read the note as if you do not already know the plan; this can reveal a missing detail. Put it in an agreed place where the reader will look.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Tell It Back
passages.text:
Story B: Tell It Back
Ezra told his sister that the club was meeting by the side gate. She repeated, "The wide gate?" Ezra shook his head and pointed to the small gate beside the shed. "Side, not wide." His sister repeated the corrected place and led him there later. Ezra was glad he had heard her version before they set out.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Adult read-aloud, not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Check a Spoken Message
passages.text:
Information B: Check a Spoken Message
After giving an important spoken direction, ask the listener to tell it back in their own words. Hearing the reply can reveal a misheard word. Correct the detail and listen again. This method needs both people to be available at the same time; a written note can be read later.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Watching a small change
passages.text:
Story A: The Ice Mark
Pia placed a small ice cube on a tray and drew around its first puddle on a scrap beneath the clear tray. She wanted to see a change immediately. For a while, she complained that nothing was happening. Her teacher suggested a short drawing break. When Pia returned, the wet area stretched beyond her mark and the cube was smaller. She made another outline and wrote LATER beside it. The quiet change had become easier to see with a record.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:

passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The Two Towers
passages.text:
Story B: The Two Towers
Kofi built two block towers. One had a wide base and one a narrow base. Before moving the tray beneath them, he drew both towers. The narrow tower fell during the gentle move, while the wide one stayed up in that trial. Kofi rebuilt the fallen tower with a wider base. He wanted to try again instead of declaring that one test answered every question.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Adult read-aloud, not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Record Two Designs
passages.text:

Draw the designs side by side and label what differs. Use the same test for both when comparing that difference. Record each result, including an unexpected one. A side-by-side record helps readers connect a design feature with the result of that particular comparison; another trial may still be useful.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Trying again with a new plan
passages.text:
Story A: The Flying Fold
Rae’s paper glider kept turning left and landing beside her feet. She wanted to throw harder, but she noticed one wing was folded higher than the other. Rae unfolded that wing carefully and matched it to the first. Her next flight reached the far edge of the rug. It still did not travel as far as she hoped, but now she had a change worth testing again. She drew the two wing positions in her notebook.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Information A: Look at the Product
When a design does not work as intended, inspect its parts. Compare matching parts to see whether they differ in a way that matters. Choose a change connected to the problem and test again. A careful look can reveal something that using more force would not fix.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The Handle Test
passages.text:
Story B: The Handle Test
Noel made a cardboard carrying box with a tiny loop handle. He could lift it with one finger, but his friend’s hand did not fit comfortably. Noel watched his friend try again, then widened the loop. Both children could carry the empty box comfortably after the change. They asked an adult before adding any weight; the new handle still needed a different test for a heavier load.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Adult read-aloud, not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Watch a User
passages.text:
Information B: Watch a User
Ask someone to try a classroom design while you observe. Notice where the person pauses, struggles, or changes their grip. These actions can reveal a problem the maker did not experience. Ask what was difficult, revise a related part, and try again. Success with one use does not prove the design works for every use.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The borrowed book’s journey
passages.text:
Moss borrowed a book with a silver moon on its cover. He read it on the steps, carried it to the kitchen, and nearly set his juice cup on it. His sister slipped a cloth beneath the cup and moved the book aside. Moss noticed a bent page corner. He wanted to flatten it quickly, but remembered the librarian’s request to report damage. At school, he showed the corner and explained what had happened. The librarian thanked him for telling her. Together they placed a paper marker at his stopping place before he borrowed the book again.
Illustration panel, fully described: The book lies on a dry desk. A narrow paper marker extends from its top. A cup stands on a separate mat beyond the book.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Sharing a Classroom Book
Choose a book you want to explore. An adult can read difficult parts with you. Keep the book away from wet food and drinks. Use a flat paper marker instead of folding a page to save your place. If you notice damage, tell the adult who manages the books. Return the book to its labeled place so another reader can find it. These steps help many readers use one collection.
Illustration panel, fully described: A low shelf has spaces labeled STORIES and INFORMATION. A return basket sits beside it, marked PLEASE CHECK IN.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The garden’s second plan
passages.text: The class planned to paint signs beside the garden beds, but a morning storm left the outdoor tables wet. Ellis said they should cancel the job. Rina looked at the unused indoor art table. "The signs don’t need to begin in the garden," she said. The children carried clean trays of materials inside and painted there. While the signs dried, they drew a placement map. The next day, an adult helped them put each sign beside its bed. Ellis read BEANS aloud and grinned. The work had moved, but its purpose had stayed the same.

Plan a Shared Task
Start by naming the job’s purpose. Then list the materials and choose a suitable place to work. Give each person a clear role, such as gathering, making, or checking. If weather or space changes, return to the purpose and ask which parts of the plan can change. Keep any necessary adult help in the new plan. At the end, check whether the work does what it was meant to do.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Building a town together
passages.text:
Every child made one building for the cardboard town. Inez built a tall library, and Dev made a bright blue bakery. When the models were placed together, the bakery stood across the road to the library. Dev did not want to move his favorite building. Inez rolled a tiny delivery cart along the road until it bumped the bakery wall. Dev looked at the blocked cart, then shifted the bakery to the side. Now the road connected both doors.
Illustration panel, fully described: A top-down town map shows a road from the gate to the library. The bakery stands beside the road with a short path joining its door. Two arrows show the cart’s route to each building.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Plan the Spaces Between
A model town needs useful spaces between buildings as well as buildings themselves. Draw paths before fixing models in place. Check whether a traveler can reach each door. Leaving a connected route can make the whole town work, even if one building must move from its maker’s first choice.
Illustration panel, fully described: Two layouts contain the same three buildings. In Layout A, one building covers the only road. In Layout B, all three stand beside a connected road.
Caption: The buildings stay the same; their arrangement changes.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The classroom collection
passages.text: Yara brought a smooth wooden spoon to the classroom collection. "It must be hundreds of years old," Finn announced because its handle looked worn. Yara shook her head. Her uncle had made it last winter, and her family used it often. Finn rubbed his thumb over the shallow groove. "So worn doesn’t always mean ancient," he said. They wrote a new label: WOODEN SPOON. MADE LAST WINTER. USED IN YARA’S HOME. Beneath it they added a question: HOW DOES USING AN OBJECT CHANGE IT? Their display had become more interesting after they stopped pretending to know everything.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Write an Honest Object Label
First name what the object is. Add details you can directly observe, such as its material, color, or shape. If its owner gives information about when or how it was made, say where that information came from. Keep an unanswered question separate from facts. A worn surface may suggest use, but appearance alone does not give an exact age. A useful label helps a viewer know both what is known and what is still uncertain.

weeks.objective: Compare characters’ experiences and explain a central message with evidence.

connection.before: Use the earlier work on retell how information is found and distinguish a topic from unsupported guesses. Review any word-reading error before adding this week's pattern.
connection.after: Next, use this evidence and word-reading routine to retell, compare, and read with meaning while choosing the next learning step.

days: Day 1: Adult models the focal sound-spelling work: Consolidate ing forms with unchanged bases, doubled consonants, and dropped silent e. Contrast tapping/taping and hopping/hoping in speech and spelling. Reread to check whether the vowel sound fits the spelling rather than guessing from the scene. Map friend explicitly with ie representing short e. Read the story aloud once for enjoyment, then discuss its central situation.
Day 2: Use worksheet A in short sessions. Adult previews only explicitly listed exceptions, listens to the student passage, and records accuracy separately from listening comprehension.
Day 3: Reread the story aloud. Work through the comprehension model, then choose worksheet B tasks; accept pointing, oral responses, drawings with labels, or brief writing.

Day 4: Adult reads the information selection and any accompanying panel descriptions aloud. Use worksheet C to connect its details to compare characters’ experiences and explain a central message with evidence.

Day 5: Student rereads the controlled passage for meaning and phrasing. Revisit one difficult word and one evidence question from each genre; compare with the first reading and name the next teaching need.
explanation: A welcoming action is useful when it responds to the other person’s need. The two stories share that idea but show different needs: a quiet introduction and an accessible explanation of a routine. Compare each character’s beginning and ending before proposing a shared message. The information paragraph’s main topic should include listening as well as acting.

Consolidate ing forms with unchanged bases, doubled consonants, and dropped silent e. Contrast tapping/taping and hopping/hoping in speech and spelling. Reread to check whether the vowel sound fits the spelling rather than guessing from the scene. Map friend explicitly with ie representing short e. Preview coming from irregular come with e dropped; setting doubles t. Review to and friend as mapped words. Explain that taping means using tape and preserves tape’s long a.

Adult guidance: Read the literary and information selections yourself, preserving their richer language; never label them decodable because a child can discuss them. In A welcome that changes, ask the learner to point to the words that support an answer after hearing them again. A reasonable interpretation can use different wording, but an invented detail is not evidence. Say the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary, then return to the sentence. During the separate student reading, prompt the child to examine letters and blend, supply a word whose pattern is untaught, and reread the sentence. Record supplied words and self-corrections; do not use a picture to guess. These short selections support practice, not a claim of comprehensive grade-level text complexity or a complete reading program.

examples.prompt: Watch your adult read taping. Explain how the sounds and spellings work together.
examples.answer: taping retains long a; it is not tapping from short-a tap.
steps: Point through the complete written word taping from left to right.
Say the sound units in order: tape + ing → taping. Blend them without inserting an extra vowel.
taping retains long a; it is not tapping from short-a tap. Reread the whole word to connect the analysis to normal speech.

examples.prompt: What shared message fits both welcomes?
examples.answer: Sample: Helpful welcoming means noticing what someone needs and adjusting support.
steps: Ada changes a crowded welcome into a quiet tour.
Niko changes pointing into walking and showing a label.
Each response works because it addresses the particular person’s difficulty.

passages.title: STUDENT controlled practice: A welcome that changes
passages.text: A friend is coming to play. Jen is making a game. Tim is setting cups on a tray. Jen is taping a line. Tim is waiting at the gate.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Independent only after the listed sound-spelling patterns and preview words have been taught.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: A welcome that changes
passages.text:
Story A: The Quiet Tour
When Suri joined the club, six children crowded around her with questions. She stared at the floor. Ada stepped back and asked, "Would you like one person to show you around?" Suri nodded. On their quiet walk, she asked where the drawing paper was kept. Soon she was making a picture beside the window. Later she introduced herself to the others one at a time. Ada learned that a welcome did not have to be loud to be warm.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Listen Before Helping
A useful welcome begins by noticing and asking. Someone may need a quiet space, a clear explanation, or time to watch. Offer a choice when possible, then listen to the answer. Check afterward whether the help was useful. The same action does not fit everyone, because people can need different kinds of support in the same place.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The Lunch Routine
passages.text:
Story B: The Lunch Routine
Bram was ready to eat but did not know where the class put empty lunch boxes. Niko pointed across the noisy room. Bram still looked puzzled. Niko walked with him to the shelf and showed the picture label of a lunch box. After lunch, Bram found the shelf by himself. The next morning he showed its label to another new child.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Adult read-aloud, not a controlled decoding text.

items.prompt: Say tap slowly. Give its sounds in order and the number of sounds.
items.answer: t / a / p; 3 sounds.

steps: Look through every spelling in running, making, sitting; do not sort only by first letter.
The matching group is running and sitting. Relevant property: double a final consonant before ing; making drops silent e.

items.answer: friend: f and r begin the word; ie represents short e, followed by n and d.
steps: Say the whole word friend and compare its sounds with its written letters.

items.answer: Read the words as printed, preserving meaning and the end mark. Sample reflection: I checked a sound and then reread smoothly. A specific accurate reflection is acceptable; speed is not the goal.

items.prompt: What is Jen using tape to make?
items.answer: A line.

worksheets.directions: Adult reads the ADULT READ-ALOUD story and any second story aloud. Answer using those supplied texts; oral answers and evidence-based alternatives are welcome.

items.prompt: What tells Ada that the crowded welcome may not suit Suri?
items.answer: Suri stares at the floor and then agrees to a one-person tour.
steps: Her reaction and answer provide evidence.
Ada checks rather than assuming every child enjoys a crowd.

items.prompt: How does Suri eventually meet the others?
items.answer: One at a time.
steps: Story A gives this later approach.
The quieter start does not mean she never joins anyone.

items.prompt: What practical question does Suri ask during the tour?
items.answer: Where the drawing paper is kept.
steps: The story names her question.
Finding that resource helps her begin an activity.

items.prompt: Why is Niko’s first help insufficient?
items.answer: Pointing across the noisy room leaves Bram puzzled.
steps: Story B describes the puzzled response.
Niko then supplies a clearer demonstration.

items.prompt: How does the shelf label help Bram later?
items.answer: He can recognize the shelf and find it himself.
steps: Niko shows the picture label, and Bram returns independently.
The label provides a stable clue.
items.skill: Compare characters’ experiences and explain a central message with evidence.

items.prompt: How do the two endings show growing participation differently?
items.answer: Suri introduces herself one at a time; Bram helps another new child find the shelf.
steps: Each ending goes beyond receiving help.
The specific forms of participation differ.

items.prompt: State a main topic broad enough for the whole passage.
items.answer: Finding out what welcome or help a person needs.
steps: The passage begins with noticing and ends with different support needs.
Only quiet spaces would leave out explanations and watching.
items.skill: Compare characters’ experiences and explain a central message with evidence.

items.prompt: Name two possible needs the passage lists.
items.answer: Any two: quiet space, clear explanation, time to watch.
steps: The second sentence supplies these examples.
They are alternatives, not a required sequence for everyone.

items.prompt: Why should the helper listen after offering a choice?
items.answer: The answer indicates what the person wants or needs.
steps: The directions connect offering and listening.
A choice is not useful if the answer is ignored.
items.skill: Compare characters’ experiences and explain a central message with evidence.

items.prompt: What should happen after help is offered?
items.answer: Check whether it was useful.
steps: The fourth sentence gives this step.
The helper should use the recipient’s response as evidence.
items.skill: Compare characters’ experiences and explain a central message with evidence.

items.prompt: Why can the same action fail to suit everyone?
items.answer: People can need different kinds of support in the same place.
steps: The final sentence gives this reason.
A shared setting does not make needs identical.
items.skill: Compare characters’ experiences and explain a central message with evidence.

items.prompt: Which story action best illustrates checking and adjusting help?
items.answer: Sample: Niko sees Bram still puzzled, then walks to the shelf with him; Ada’s question and quieter tour also fit.
steps: The chosen action responds to a learner’s reaction.
Accept either story with the specific response and adjustment named.

Read unfamiliar combinations using taught units, then verify meaning in the sentence. Review the irregular words that actually caused difficulty rather than adding a long untested memorization list. Read the story aloud once for enjoyment, then discuss its central situation.
Day 2: Use worksheet A in short sessions. Adult previews only explicitly listed exceptions, listens to the student passage, and records accuracy separately from listening comprehension.
Day 3: Reread the story aloud. Work through the comprehension model, then choose worksheet B tasks; accept pointing, oral responses, drawings with labels, or brief writing.

Day 5: Student rereads the controlled passage for meaning and phrasing. Revisit one difficult word and one evidence question from each genre; compare with the first reading and name the next teaching need.
explanation: A final retelling should preserve the change that makes the ending meaningful. Here the celebration succeeds through more than one kind of reading participation, so a message about fastest reading would miss the evidence. Compare the two information notices by purpose and details, then make a supported recommendation. The adult should keep a specific record of independent decoding, supplied words, phrasing, and comprehension instead of awarding mastery from one short passage.

Cumulative review: short vowels, digraphs, clusters, final-e, ai/ay, ee/ea, oa/ow, two-syllable parts, and s/es/ed/ing. Read unfamiliar combinations using taught units, then verify meaning in the sentence. Review the irregular words that actually caused difficulty rather than adding a long untested memorization list. Preview new as /n/ + /oo/ (or /nyoo/ in some dialects), since ew is not part of the earlier sequence. Preview reading as read /reed/ + ing; in then read a page, read is past-tense /red/. Preview page with soft g /j/. Preview picked as pick + ed /t/. went is a regular short-e cluster word. Adult records help on these transfer words.

Adult guidance: Read the literary and information selections yourself, preserving their richer language; never label them decodable because a child can discuss them. In The reading celebration, ask the learner to point to the words that support an answer after hearing them again. A reasonable interpretation can use different wording, but an invented detail is not evidence. Say the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary, then return to the sentence. During the separate student reading, prompt the child to examine letters and blend, supply a word whose pattern is untaught, and reread the sentence. Record supplied words and self-corrections; do not use a picture to guess. These short selections support practice, not a claim of comprehensive grade-level text complexity or a complete reading program.

examples.prompt: Watch your adult read raincoats. Explain how the sounds and spellings work together.
examples.answer: raincoats has two syllables; the plural s adds /s/ without another vowel beat.
steps: Point through the complete written word raincoats from left to right.
Say the sound units in order: rain / coat + s. Blend them without inserting an extra vowel.
raincoats has two syllables; the plural s adds /s/ without another vowel beat. Reread the whole word to connect the analysis to normal speech.

examples.prompt: Why do the teacher’s three headings fit the celebration better than FASTEST READER?
examples.answer: The children show word reading, story understanding, and different next practice needs.
steps: Amaya reads practised parts and receives help on a hard sentence.
Ellis demonstrates understanding by retelling the ending.
The three headings recognize distinct evidence instead of reducing success to speed.

passages.title: STUDENT controlled practice: The reading celebration
passages.text: Gail packed a book and a raincoat. She went to the reading tent. Ben was reading. Gail waited, then read a page. They smiled and picked a new book.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Independent only after the listed sound-spelling patterns and preview words have been taught.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: The reading celebration
passages.text: The class planned a reading celebration with a chair for the reader and a rug for listeners. Amaya wanted to read her whole story aloud, but she stumbled over a long word and closed the book. Theo offered to share the reading. Amaya read the parts she had practised, and Theo read the difficult sentence with her. Afterward, a quiet child named Ellis retold the ending so clearly that everyone looked back at the final picture. The teacher wrote three headings on the board: WORDS WE READ, IDEAS WE UNDERSTAND, NEXT THINGS TO PRACTISE. There was room beneath every heading for every child.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original literary text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Related information
passages.text:
Notice A: Choose a Reading Partner
Read a short part together before choosing how to share a book. One person may read a line and the other the next line. A partner can supply an unfamiliar word, but the learner should then look at its spelling and reread the sentence. Talk about what happened or what was learned. Record help honestly so the next practice fits the learner.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original informational text; adult reads aloud. Not a controlled decoding text.

passages.title: ADULT READ-ALOUD: Choose a Book to Hear
passages.text:
Notice B: Choose a Book to Hear
An adult read-aloud can offer language and ideas beyond a child’s current decoding. Choose a story or information text that invites questions and discussion. Pause to clarify a needed word, then continue so the whole text still makes sense. Listening understanding and independent word reading are useful but different evidence; keep both in the learning record.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Adult read-aloud, not a controlled decoding text.

items.prompt: Retell the celebration’s central change.
items.answer: Amaya stops after a hard word; Theo shares the reading; Ellis adds a clear retelling; the teacher records different strengths and next steps.

A complete account includes understanding as well as reading words.

items.answer: Sample: Readers can help one another and show learning in different ways while continuing to practise.

items.prompt: Which notice focuses on taking turns reading printed words?
items.answer: Notice A.
steps: It gives alternating-line and supplied-word routines.
Notice B focuses on hearing an adult read.

items.answer: Look at the spelling and reread the sentence.

items.answer: They can offer language and ideas beyond current decoding.

Listening opens access without labeling the text independently decodable.

items.prompt: What do both notices value beyond saying words?
items.answer: Understanding: A asks what happened or was learned; B invites questions and discussion.

Reading practice is not only speed or pronunciation.

items.prompt: How should adult help affect the learning record?
items.answer: It should be recorded honestly and distinguished from independent reading.

This supports a suitable next step rather than overstating independence.

items.prompt: Choose a notice for a child who wants a rich story but cannot yet decode its words; give a reason.
items.answer: Notice B, because an adult can read the richer language and discuss it. Notice A could supplement separate accessible word practice.
steps: B directly addresses ideas beyond current decoding.
The recommendation matches the stated need, not a claim that partner reading is never useful.
